n: Book Three of the Psalms opens with Asaph, a chief musician of David’s time, stating the truth he nearly lost hold of: God really is good to the pure in heart.

f.w: such as are of a clean heart

f.g: Surely, indeed — a conclusion reached after struggle.

n: “But as for me” — he confesses that his faith almost slipped out from under him.

f.w: my steps had well nigh slipped
f.g: My feet almost lost their footing.

n: The cause: he grew envious when he saw arrogant, wicked people doing well. This is one of scripture’s most honest treatments of a common struggle.

f.w: I was envious at the foolish

n: They seemed to live without pain and die without struggle; their bodies were healthy and strong.

f.w: there are no bands in their death
f.g: They have no pangs — no struggles, even at death.

n: They didn’t seem to have the troubles everyone else has.
So they wear pride like a necklace and violence like clothing — proudly displayed.

f.w: pride compasseth them about as a chain

n: Their eyes bulge from overeating; they have more than they could ever imagine wanting.
They mock and speak with malice, threatening oppression from their lofty position.

f.g: Talk down arrogantly from on high.

n: Their mouths claim heaven and their tongues swagger across the earth — no limit to their arrogance.
Even God’s own people turn toward them and drink in their words as if from an overflowing cup. The Hebrew is difficult here.

f.w: waters of a full cup are wrung out to them
f.g: They soak up abundant water — likely, they eagerly accept the arrogant’s message.

n: The arrogant say, “How could God know? Does the Most High even notice?”
Here they are: wicked, always comfortable, always getting richer.
The low point: Asaph wonders if keeping his heart pure and his hands clean has been pointless.

f.w: I have cleansed my heart in vain

n: Meanwhile he suffers all day and is disciplined every morning.
Yet he realizes that if he spoke this way openly, he would betray the community of believers. He keeps his doubts from harming others.

f.w: offend against the generation of thy children

n: When he tried to figure it out on his own, it only wore him out.
The turning point of the psalm: in God’s sanctuary, he finally understood how the story ends for the wicked. Perspective often comes in the house of the Lord.

f.w: Until I went into the sanctuary of God

n: God has set the wicked on slippery ground; they are headed for ruin. Asaph’s feet nearly slipped (verse 2), but theirs certainly will.
How suddenly they are ruined, swept away by terrors!
Their success is like a dream that vanishes when one wakes. When God rises up, their image dissolves.

f.w: As a dream when one awaketh

n: Looking back, Asaph admits his bitterness had soured his heart and stung his inner self.

f.g: Kidneys — the seat of deep emotions.

n: He was senseless, acting like a dumb animal before God.

f.g: Like a brute animal without understanding.

n: “Nevertheless” — even then, God never let go. Asaph realizes God had been holding his right hand all along.

f.w: thou hast holden me by my right hand

n: God will guide him with counsel in this life and afterward receive him into glory — one of the Old Testament’s clearest hopes of life with God after death.
The heart of the psalm: whom do I have in heaven but you? And on earth, there is nothing I desire besides you. Wealth no longer looks so appealing.

f.w: Whom have I in heaven but thee?

n: His body and heart may fail, but God is his strength and his inheritance forever.

f.g: My share, inheritance — as the Levites had God instead of land.

n: Those who wander far from God will perish; those who are unfaithful to him will be destroyed.

f.g: Be unfaithful — scripture often pictures idolatry as betraying a marriage covenant.

n: His conclusion: for me, it is good to be near God. He has made the Lord his refuge so he can tell of all God’s works.

f.w: it is good for me to draw near to God
